segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Janah Boccio's Health and Human Relations class, they're studying puberty now. And for the entire period, the sixth-grade boys are a squirming, moving, fidgeting, chatty mess.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [STUDENTS LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And can I say, as they get deeper into the material, they do not seem to see much of an upside to puberty at all, anywhere. When they notice that one of the books uses the word "enjoyable" to describe sex, one boy declares...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I don't think so. That's disgusting.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: Why are you saying that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Because it's disgusting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when Miss Boccio asked the boys if they're looking forward to any part of puberty--

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Growing in height, not anything else.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A lot of things are growing.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: So is there anything that you're not looking forward to?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah--

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I'm not looking forward to pubic hair.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Because it might be weird.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: What else are you not looking forward to?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sweating more, a lot more.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Chest hair. Chest hair.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Getting really smelly.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: Chest hair.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sweating like a moose.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: You're going to smell more bad. You're going to sweat. Your shirt is going to get all sweaty. It's going to get worse.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah, because when I was younger, it didn't smell like this.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I know, it smelled nice. You smelled better. Now, you smell bad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They said that shaving seems like it's going to be a drag, which, by the way, good call, kids. Several boys squealed that the illustration of pubic hair in the book looked like burnt macaroni and cheese. Near the end of class, one of the kids, Jack, told me that part of what's so freaky is that you just don't know when puberty is going to strike you.

segments.speaker: Jack
segments.text: It's scary because it's not like a set date and time. It can happen when you're 8 or happen when you're 16. So you're not 100% prepared. It's like a mysterious monster. You know it's going to get you.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's going to hit you at one point.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it's like, you know that there's this thing that's coming to get you. You don't know when it's going to be, and you're going to be totally different on the other side of it.

segments.speaker: Jack
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: On the opposite end of the country, in Northern California, 10-year-old Paris was at a similar class, a class about puberty for moms and girls. And she described the approaching monster in different terms that got across pretty much the same idea.

segments.speaker: Paris
segments.text: It's a little scary, almost. I guess it's a little like on the edge of a cliff. Like, there's a really good movie coming out, and you're just about to see it. But people say that it can be either bad or good, and you're not really sure which.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Paris told the reporter that she talked to, Marianne McCune, that she was one of the first ones in her class to hit puberty, which of course is not fun. Like most kids, I think, she did not like looking different from everybody else.

segments.speaker: Paris
segments.text: It's like, you don't want it to happen. You want your body to stay the same. You don't want your body to look gross. And so it's kind of gross being different. Yeah, I really didn't want to.

segments.speaker: Marianne Mccune
segments.text: Did you think there might be a way out?

segments.speaker: Paris
segments.text: No, I didn't think there was going to be a way out. I was hoping that there would be some type of medicine or something that I could take, and it would go away. But no, it didn't really work that way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A lot of kids feel this way. In these classes, they ask the teachers, why does this have to happen, and is there any way I can stay a kid? It's crazy to be told you can't do anything about this. It's coming. And when it happens, everything will be different. How many things in our lives are like that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today, on our show, we have stories of people dealing with the inevitable, trying to do their best, trying to stay themselves through these things that can be so confusing and potentially soul-crushing. And we're not going to mess around today with little inevitable things in life, with traffic and relatives you don't like and what happens if you never brush your teeth.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: No, no, no. We're going to go with the big ones. We're going to go with two inescapable things that are absolutely certain. Act 1 of our show is about death. Act 2 is about taxes. These are two things that are unavoidable, that actually I think most of us don't know that much about. And today we turn to people who know more than us. Prepare to be surprised at what they say.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Death. So we can only guess at what happens to us after we die, but we do not have to guess at what happens right before. Though most of us remain ignorant until we arrive at that moment ourselves, Nancy Updike found a spot where she could understand all this better. Here's Nancy.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Before I tell you where I went, let me tell you why I wanted to go. Four years ago, my mother's husband, Asa, was dying. She was taking care of him at home with help from a hospice. And I went to be with her and him for the last 10 days of his life.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: He was this tall, very funny man with beautiful manners who adored my mother. I felt clumsy and helpless all the time in those last days-- with Asa, with my mom. I didn't know what to say to someone who's dying. I didn't know how to be. I'm sure that's true for lots of people.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I remember checking in on Asa one afternoon and asking him if he needed anything. He looked at me and said, I need everything. We both laughed. That was the closest I ever got to talking with him about what was happening.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: There were people around who did know what to do, though-- the nurses. I watched them from my stupor of awkwardness. They never brought any false cheer into the room with Asa, which is hard not to do with a dying person. They were direct. When Jackie, the weekend day nurse, left the Sunday before Asa died, she said to him, is it OK if I kiss your hand? And then she said, God willing, I'll see you next week.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The nurses knew how to deal with us, the rest of the family, too. One of the nurses, Jenny, got me cleaning out the fridge one morning. We did it together for an hour and a half, just talking, passing the time. It wasn't until later that I realized, oh, she did that for me, to give me something to do. It was a strange feeling to know I was that transparent to her.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: For the last hour of Asa's life, the people in the room were my mother, one of Asa's sons, Jenny, and me. We held Asa's hands. Jenny was standing, and she sometimes touched Asa's head gently. She told him, it's all right. It's OK. Your family is OK. Everyone is all right. Asa's eyes were open. They'd been that way all day. He was staring up and to the right, over our heads. He didn't see us. He moaned every once in a while, and we spoke to him when he moaned. The four of us watched his breathing slow down and get shallower until he was taking just sips of air.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: When he was very close to the end, Jenny brought over a glass of water and a little dropper that we'd been using to moisten Asa's mouth. And she told us each to take the dropper and give him some water and say our names close to his ear so that he would know who was giving him each bit of water. As a ritual, it felt comforting and sad and vaguely religious. And Asa's son and I were both crying. I had no idea how badly we'd needed a ritual at that moment until Jenny gave us one.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I had never seen the kind of expertise these nurses had. They knew death. They seemed to understand it, whereas I-- even though I had just watched someone fade away and die right in front of me, all I could think was, what just happened?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: But I didn't realize how much of a hold all of this had on me still until I heard a stranger talking a few months ago about how his mother is a nurse who works in a hospice facility, seeing people die almost every day.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And then he went on to say that after his mother had worked there for a few months, she forgot the president's name. And when she mentioned that to her boss, her boss said, yeah, that happens. That's normal here. Your brain is blocking out a lot of what you're seeing, and some other stuff is getting blocked, too. My first thought was, my god, of course. They're experts, not robots. My second thought was, I need to go to this place and talk to these people.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Oop, this guy wants to pass me. Usually, nobody ever passes me. I'm on my best behavior with you in the car. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: So this is Pattie Burnham. She's the one who forgot the president's name. That was five years ago, though. She's on top of it now. It's Barack Obama, by the way. Pattie is a registered nurse, and the place she works is an inpatient hospice about 30 minutes north of Boston called the Kaplan Family Hospice House. We're driving there now. Pattie's got a double shift today. I told her my whole backstory so she knows why I'm here.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie is 5'8", blonde, full of energy, even though it's 6:00 AM. She's lived in this part of Massachusetts her whole life, worked at a hospital, then as a nurse at her kids' school. And then when they graduated, she was looking for another job, and she went to the Kaplan House.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I pulled into the parking lot and thought, wow, this place is beautiful. And then I noticed, off to the left, there's sort of a back entrance, a garage entrance. And there were two funeral-home cars pulled up there waiting. And I just sat in the parking lot, staring at the house and staring at the cars and wondering what could possibly be going on in that building.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Hospice can mean a building, like Kaplan, or home care, like Asa had. They both mean the same thing. The patient is not looking to be cured. It's palliative care for people at the end of their life.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The Kaplan House actually is beautiful. All the rooms have big windows. The lobby and main common area have vaulted ceilings and skylights. Nothing is covered in plastic. I overheard one family member of a patient say, the thing I like about this place is, there isn't a phony plant in here. All the flowers are real. There's a big kitchen for any patients who can still eat. Pattie speed-walks by.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I need a fruit cup for room 4, please and thank you.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This is not just a place for rich people with private insurance. Lots of patients are on Medicare or Medicaid. Kaplan House is run by a nonprofit called Care Dimensions, and the bulk of what they do is home care. Kaplan House has rooms for just 20 patients. And it's not full today, but Pattie is busy. She rushes between rooms and then slows down as soon as she steps inside one.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Does she look comfortable to you?

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie is talking to Crystal, the daughter of a 51-year-old woman named Lori who came to Kaplan House a few hours ago. She has lung cancer. It's metastasized to her brain. Lori is delirious, making sounds but not speaking much anymore. Her family has been taking care of her at home. They tell Pattie that Lori always liked to look good. She has a perfect red manicure and pedicure.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Yeah, you've been taking beautiful care of her. She looks beautiful.

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: [SNIFFLES]

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: If you want to chat about anything, if you have any questions about the medications or what's going on--

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: --we can step outside. And you might not have any questions now, but they might come up.

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Right, yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Right?

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Yup.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The questions do come up. Crystal comes and finds Pattie, and she does something I remember doing. Crystal starts out asking about one small, specific thing to try and get a handle on what's happening. She wants to know, what is the tube that's on her mother's face right under her nose? She asks so quietly it's hard to hear. But she says, what's that thing on her nose? She smells like bleach.

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: What's that thing on her nose? She smells like bleach.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Oxygen. That's just oxygen, yeah.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This question-- basically, what is that thing on my mother's face that is making her look and smell like she's not my mother? That's just the first in a giant, unsorted pile of questions about what's happening and why, and what am I supposed to be doing and feeling? Crystal says some of the family and friends in the room have been saying that no one should touch Lori.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Not to touch her?

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: You can touch her.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: From there, she tells Pattie, in one long, crying sentence, that people in the room have been telling her mother that it's OK to let go. And one of the times someone said it, her mother all of a sudden said, no. And what does that mean, since she's delirious?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And should I be saying it's OK for her to let go? In some ways, I wish she would let go so she wouldn't suffer anymore, but I feel weird even thinking that. And my mom has gotten close to the end like this a few times before, and then she's come back. And maybe that's what's happening. And some people in the room are saying you guys are drugging her so that she'll die faster. And I don't know about any of this. I don't know. Pattie listens to the whole thing and then jumps in.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: So a lot of people, Crystal, ask these questions. We are not drugging her to put her to sleep. I wouldn't do this job if that was the case. Your mom, I'm sorry to say, is dying. She has started her dying process. This is what-- everything you're seeing is part of the dying process.

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Because I know they keep saying, she's going to die. And she's done this, like, three or four times and got through it. And I'm just wondering what--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: So the things I'm seeing that makes me think that it's this time-- this is the time-- is her heart is beating really, really fast and just fluttering. You can't feel a good, strong pulse out here. Her legs and her hands are cold. Her feet-- it's showing a telltale sign that we see called mottling, where the feet and the knees get dappled, like little purplish marks. And it just means her body is conserving all her blood to be around here.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I would bet my nursing license that your mother is not going to turn around from this. But if her body is meant to turn around, I'm not giving her anything that won't allow her to turn around. Does that make sense to you?

segments.speaker: Crystal
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I remember standing with my mother and one of Asa's nurses in the kitchen and having this conversation, the this-is-it conversation. There are so many stages to a long decline-- dips and resurgences and good days. And you know-- you know it's all the same thing. It's all dying. But there's a huge difference between dying and the very last part of dying, what Pattie and the other nurses call actively dying, a process that can take hours or even days. But it's different from what comes before. And being familiar with one doesn't mean you'll recognize the other.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I talked to Pattie later, and I asked her how she knows when someone is actively dying. How does she know it so well that she would say, I'd bet my nursing license that this is what's happening?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I don't always feel that way. Yeah. It's a weird thing, because when I came to work at the Kaplan House-- and I was a registered nurse and had worked as a nurse for a while-- I followed another nurse, Jeannette, for a month. And I was floored by the whole dying process, because it was nothing that I had learned.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: And I saw Jeanette say to a family-- she woke them up and said, he's dying. He's dying right now. And the man had been there-- the patient had been there for a week. And I didn't know what was different. I didn't know what she saw that was different. And when I asked her to explain it to me and to teach it to me, she said, you'll know. You just need about a month here, and you'll know.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I talked to a palliative-care doctor who told me that the most important thing she got better at with experience was looking for openings that allow you to be helpful-- little windows, little moments. With hospice, part of that is trying to help people take in, bit by bit, the realness of what's happening.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Some dying people, no surprise, are not at all OK with the fact that they're dying. And they don't often get a chance to just say so. I saw a home-care nurse talking to a man, a former math teacher in his 60s. She was talking about antidepressants, asking him whether he was depressed. He thought about it, and he said, well, I'm not "jump out the window" depressed, more like, what the fuck happened?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Asa was a courtly man. I never heard him swear or even speak harshly in my life. But I could tell how frustrated he was sometimes by the sheer logistics of being a dying person, the imposition of it. Sometimes just the question, do you want this, seemed overwhelming. Dying is a constant series of judgment calls and decisions based on options that are very far from what anyone would want. And one thing the nurses are experienced at is trying to make the best of those narrow options.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Joanne, it is no bother, first of all. And Christiana and I were going to do it together. I would love to give you a shower before you head home.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie is crouching next to a woman named Joanne, who's going home later today. She has lung cancer, and she's been getting hospice care at home. But her pain got worse, so she came to the Kaplan House for a few days of round-the-clock supervision while the doctors adjusted her pain medications.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: People sometimes come in and out of Kaplan House like this. They're dying, but they still have time left in their lives. And the staff tries to get their symptoms under control-- pain or vomiting or whatever it is-- so that they can do more with that time than just be sick.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This room smells bad. It's strong. Joanne hasn't been able to shower in a little while. She said she has a hard time doing it at home. She's tiny in the bed, barely looking up, talking almost inaudibly. But her strength of will is intact. She knows the ambulance can't pick her up and take her home until later, but she wants to be home now, already. And anything that isn't going home is something she doesn't want to do, even though, a couple of hours ago, she was glad when Pattie suggested a shower, because it's much easier to do here when two people can get on either side of her and steady her.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I just feel like this is such a great opportunity, because it's so hard to do at home, and there's two of us here.

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Why can't I take a shower in my own shower?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Do you do that regularly at home? Or is it hard because you need two people? Because you were telling me you don't feel that safe with the left side.

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Yeah, but I do have-- what do you call it? I have that--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: The bar that you hold onto and stuff, yeah. Want a back rub or--

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Yeah, maybe a neck rub.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: OK, OK. Yeah, it helps with your pain. We could put some lotion. Can we wash your back?

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Want to head into the bathroom? And you can sit on this in the bathroom. OK, let's do that.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Maybe you can tell where Pattie is going with this. I'd seen her taking care of Joanne and others all day, people clearly in the midst of some of the worst days of their lives-- afraid, in pain, sick of being sick. And it takes serious skills to be able to nudge somebody in that situation toward a thing that they don't think they want but are very glad when they get it.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Can we take your pants down so she can get your backside?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: [SHUFFLING]

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: All right, is that a comfortable position for you? Joanne, you do know we're getting pretty close to a shower.

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: You sure you don't-- look at how--

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Go ahead.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Go ahead. Whoo-hoo! Whoo-hoo!

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Joanne's husband, Larry, had been sitting quietly in the room this whole time. He had agreed that a shower was a good idea, but he didn't want to push Joanne on it. And then he seemed happy when she decided to do it. Once she was in, both he and Joanne relaxed a bit. Joanne joked around with Pattie in the shower, and Larry got up to leave and go home to get the house ready for when Joanne got back. They've been married 27 years.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Do you want to give him a grocery list or anything, Joanne?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Little honey-do list before you get there?

segments.speaker: Joanne
segments.text: Love you, hon.

segments.speaker: Larry
segments.text: I love you, too. See you soon.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Your tailbone is sore? All right, we'll make sure to get that.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: There's a note on the Medicare website about hospice, saying, hospice isn't just for cancer. I saw people at Kaplan House with other conditions-- end-stage dementia, congestive heart failure. But mostly I saw cancer. Asa had cancer.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: At the Kaplan House, I realized I had questions about the physical part of what had happened with him. I saw other people who had that extreme cancer thinness I learned the medical term-- cachectic. It's from Greek words that mean bad condition. In a few rooms, I saw the same swabs, these little green sponges on the end of a stick, that we used to keep Asa's mouth clean and moist.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The swabs stayed with me because I remember being grateful that they gave us a way-- a small way-- we could care for Asa even after he'd stopped being able to tell us what he wanted. That was the hardest time-- for me, at least-- to hear him groaning and not know what to do or not do. We grilled the nurses about what they thought was going on and what we should do. And at the Kaplan House, I saw that a significant part of the nurses' jobs is trying to figure out what a person might need when they can't communicate anymore.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Are you having pain? Does something hurt?

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie is back in Lori's room, Crystal's mother. It's nighttime. We're into the double part of Pattie's double shift. And Lori is moving around a lot in the bed. It sounds terrible to say, but I felt comforted to see it and to see others at Kaplan House do it, too, because I'd seen it with Asa.

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Apparently, it's common toward the end. It's called terminal agitation. Lori's family hasn't slept in 24 hours because Lori was up all night last night, delirious, moving, sometimes trying to get out of bed, even though she's too weak to stand and could easily break a bone if she falls. It's exhausting to deal with and hard to watch.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The problem with agitation, as a palliative-care doctor told me, is that it isn't a diagnosis. It's something you see, but the person can be doing it for lots of reasons, each of which calls for a different approach. They could be constipated, anxious, in pain, some combination. A dying person is like a baby that way, except we know even less about a dying person's brain than we do about a baby's.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Some of the guesses we make are based on what we know from coma patients. But a dying brain is not a comatose brain. It's different. And in terms of what a dying person perceives, someone who's non-responsive, the science of it-- we know almost nothing. The nurses told me they assume that people can hear us right to the end, but no one knows for sure.

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Lori's eyes are open, but it's that distant stare like Asa had. She's not seeing what's in front of her. Her mouth is open, and she's squirming in the bed. She was a sign-language interpreter, and sometimes she seems to be signing. But no one in the room knows what she's saying, if anything.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: You want to tell us something.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie is right up close, talking to Lori, watching her face. It's something I saw the nurses do with Asa, too-- get right up close and talk to him and watch his face, even after he seemed to have stopped responding, because sometimes, suddenly, he would respond, especially to direct questions like--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Are you having pain?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: --are you in pain? Lori gives a small shake of her head and says, no.

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Oh, good. Oh, I'm glad to hear that. Yeah. Do you have to pee?

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I'm thinking of putting a catheter in to help you pee.

segments.speaker: Lori
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Yeah, I think it's probably bothering her. She hasn't peed. And yeah, I'm going to do that, OK?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie and Christiana, one of the hospice aides, put in a catheter, and the bag immediately starts filling up. Lori relaxes. The whole family relaxes. Or at least, they're able to give in to their exhaustion. Lori's girlfriend, Karen, finds Pattie in the hall.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: The cancer doctor said that she might-- chances are, she might fall asleep and die in her sleep, because--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: That's what I think.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: --the cancer doctor knew her well, too-- knew she was a toughie.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: She is a toughie.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: I think the catheter is really helping her to settle down.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: OK?

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: Yeah, I think I'm going to go home, take a shower--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: --relax as much as I can. And then--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Good, good. If I see a major change, I will call you.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: But as I said, sometimes they just sneak away.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: Yeah, I know. I'm not surprised. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Karen
segments.text: You know my number.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: You feel useless.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This is the sister of another patient. She came straight from work to be with him and has been here day and night for two days. I've been talking to her a lot. I know the strain of this waiting, where nothing is happening, and your brain keeps flitting between the giant, existential thing that's going on and the tedious nuts and bolts of just getting through every hour. Every moment seems full of meaning and yet not meaningful at all. It's surreal, and it is crazy-making.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How are you doing?

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: I'm exhausted. Yeah, I'm exhausted. It's like, what am I doing? I'm just watching him. Like, last night, all's he does is-- I'll tell you what he does. He makes this noise. It's like, [GROANS], but non-stop. So I try to do it with him. Not as loud, just-- I cannot hold it as long as he can. I'm like, this kid is not even going to stop to take a breath. Me? I'm like, [PANTS]. It's exhausting, and he can do it.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: You must really think I'm nuts. There's nothing else to do, is all. I don't know what I want to do. It's not like he can--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I'm so sorry.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: Oh, no, don't be sorry. You know what? I'm just sitting here for like-- just sitting. You can't do anything. I'm tired of praying to God. Really, I'm tired. But I told him I'd stay with him. And I don't want to-- even if he doesn't know I'm here or not, I know I'm here.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I never knew what anyone was going to say at the Kaplan House. Listening to family members in rooms and in the halls, I got the feeling that their brains were full to the brim with what was happening, and asking them any question tipped all their thoughts out in a rush.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Some people told me the whole story of their family member's diagnosis and treatment up to five minutes ago. I heard one of the doctors say to an 84-year-old woman who was sitting with her dying husband, you know him better than we do. Does he look comfortable to you? The woman responded by telling the entire story of their relationship, starting with, we met when I was 13.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The staff has a name for that kind of answer. It's called life review. They say it happens a lot. And I heard life reviews that were a lot darker than that one. Not every death is the end of a well-lived life. But all the stories seem to be trying to tackle the same huge question. How did we get here?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Grief is one thing, but watching somebody die is a whole 'nother thing.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie again.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: You know, not everybody can sit beside a dying person and hold their hand. And I think sometimes it's too much. Nobody wants their loved ones to be alone. I get that. But you could wait here for days and days, and when you go to take that one shower is when the person might die.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And sometimes people I've talked to say it's common that the person will die--

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Alone.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Well, it's almost like they're waiting for everyone to go away.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Right, right.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Is that what you've found?

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: We see that over and over and over again. When I first started working there, I'm like, this is a bit of mumbo-jumbo. [LAUGHS] And it just seemed like, come on. Now I'm repeating the same stuff that I heard people say when I first got there, because I've seen it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You mean that people die when either everyone leaves the room, or their spouse or their child or whoever has been there for a long time-- they die after that person leaves the room.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Yeah, or they're comatose, and the loved ones keep saying, he's waiting for his brother to get here on Saturday. They're coming from Florida on Saturday. And I'm, inside, rolling my eyes, thinking, it's Tuesday. He's going to die on Wednesday or Thursday. He's not going to be here on Saturday for when his brother arrives from Florida. And then the brother arrives at Logan, shows up at the Kaplan House at 12:30, and the patient dies at 1:00. And they say to me, I told you. He just needed Billy to come from Florida. And it's like, what?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Talking to people about whoever they were visiting at the Kaplan House always brought up other, earlier losses. Always. One woman who was sitting with her mother told me about how her husband had died suddenly eight years earlier, making her a widow at age 51. A woman whose younger sister was dying said she lost both parents before age 13.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: A woman visiting her brother told me about how his daughter had died years ago at only two years old. The woman said her brother was so angry about his daughter's death that he said to her, his sister, why couldn't it have been one of your effing daughters? You've got two.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: It was like a map. This death related to that death over there, linked to this living person here, a hidden geography shaping all of our lives.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: After I'd been at the Kaplan House for several days, I ran into Larry, the husband of Joanne, the woman Pattie coaxed into getting a shower before going home. Larry was sitting alone in the main common area. I knew it couldn't be good that Joanne was back so soon.

segments.speaker: Larry
segments.text: Well, the doctor was in earlier. Were you there when the doctor said she thought she had like a week or so left?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I wasn't there.

segments.speaker: Larry
segments.text: Yeah. And I figured she was closing in on it, because of the way I've watched her deteriorate. But when you hear somebody who's used to dealing with this for a living tell you that they think that's what's left, it hits home.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I'm so sorry, Larry.

segments.speaker: Larry
segments.text: [SIGHS] It's a bitter pill to swallow, but that's life. It goes on no matter what. [SIGHS]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: One of the many ways I've been a smug idiot in my life was by disparaging the use of euphemisms for death and dying. I thought it was weak. Who would do that? By the time Asa was at the end, I had barely been able to utter the words "death" or "dying" for several months. I felt like the thing itself was only manageable if I didn't invoke it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Pattie told me that one of her strategies for protecting herself at work is never to imagine herself in the place of the dying person or their family members. She tries not to picture her husband or her kids. I remember trying and failing at that.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I think part of my clumsiness around Asa and my mother was my barely-suppressed terror at the thought of my own husband dying. I pictured myself in my mother's place all the time. Every morning before going to her apartment, I pulled out a piece of paper, and I had to read the words on it out loud in order to make it out the door. "Your husband isn't dying. This is not about you. Your mother needs you. Go to her apartment now." It was my own little serenity prayer. God grant me the wisdom to know the difference between my fear and her reality.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: When I heard a woman at the Kaplan House say to her husband, who was dying of colon cancer, something like, we had a really good run until the last few months, didn't we, baby? I had to turn away to go look at a lamp in the corner.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: But I think death makes narcissists of us all at one point or another, even the pros. I was walking with a nurse named Kim. She worked in critical care for two-plus decades before changing over to hospice. We had just left one woman's room and were heading down the hall when Kim said, shaking her head--

segments.speaker: Kim
segments.text: She's 51. I'm 52.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Kim, and everyone else, said these are the cases that can be hardest to defend against-- the ones where you can't not picture yourself when you look at them. She had another just last week.

segments.speaker: Kim
segments.text: There was one woman I had my age. And she had two boys that were my age--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Your sons' ages.

segments.speaker: Kim
segments.text: My sons' ages. And the boys were very attentive. They stayed with her and just laid beside her. And it was just really-- it hit me on the way home. You think, oh my gosh, this could be me.

segments.speaker: Juliet
segments.text: It was the same age as me, I remember.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This is Juliet, one of the CNAs, Certified Nursing Assistants. She's studying to be a nurse, and she remembered the first time she had a patient her own age.

segments.speaker: Juliet
segments.text: At that time, I had just turned 39. And I'm like, oh my god. I actually said, oh my god. That's my age. Oh my god. That's me. That's me. That's me.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Sometimes they see patients their children's ages. This is Jackie, another nurse.

segments.speaker: Jackie
segments.text: We had a nine-year-old boy that was here. And my daughter, Sarah, was nine years old at the time. And I remember climbing in her bed when I went home, and I just fell asleep in her bed. And she was so mad at me, [LAUGHS] because I'm breathing on her and stealing her covers. And she was so mad. And I remember just waking up and thinking that was the funniest thing in the world-- that she was mad. But I needed to do that when I came home that night. I needed to know, my nine-year-old is OK.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Jackie also told me, while I was following her around, throwing out questions--

segments.speaker: Jackie
segments.text: Last year, I had my kidney removed because I had a big tumor in it. So--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Jackie
segments.text: --all I could think of was, oh, shit, I'm going to end up at work. [LAUGHS] But if I'm to be anywhere, that's where I wanted to be. And when one of our docs-- Dr. Warren came to see me in the hospital. And I thought, this is it. I'm dying. The hospice doc just walked in the door.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And it does happen. A nurse named Rosemary, who's been there for a long time, told me about one of the other longtime nurses, Kathleen.

segments.speaker: Rosemary
segments.text: Went out on medical leave to have her bunions fixed and was diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and just had a very rough go of it. Nothing worked. Every treatment, she had reactions to. And finally, it was time for Kathleen to come to the Kaplan House. And she was determined that she was not going to come in on a stretcher like the other patients, because she was a nurse. So she walked down the hall and greeted everybody on her way down.

segments.speaker: Rosemary
segments.text: But it was really hard for us to take care of one of our own, because I think we think, well, we're hospice nurses, so we don't get sick. And the first night, she came in, and I had her as a patient. And I came out to my med cart, and there was a note. "Dear Rosemary, could I please have a milligram of Dilaudid for 8 out of 10 pain? I know you're going to think I should have 2 milligrams, but I only want 1 milligram. No hurry. Take care of the patients first. And one face cloth and one towel when you get a chance." And that was just Kathleen.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Death and illness, who's here and who's not, how we live with this hanging over us-- these are the conversations I'd been waiting years to have. Before I left, I got to ask Pattie what it's like to talk with her patients so directly the way that I was never able to do with Asa.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: Patients all the time ask you, is this it? Am I dying? And the first thing I usually do is say, well, you might know better than me. Do you think you're dying? And usually, if it's a dying person, they say yes.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: And I'll say, are you nervous? Are you anxious? What are you afraid of? And if they say, I'm afraid I'm going to have pain, we'll just talk about it and say, well, I've got this, this, and this to give you if you have pain. So if you feel a little bit of pain, I want you to tell me. And we'll head off a little problem rather than a big problem.

segments.speaker: Pattie Burnham
segments.text: And they'll say, well, I'm afraid I'll feel like I won't be able to breathe. Then we talk about that, about the medications I'll give them. And all they have to do is tell me they're short of breath, and they get the medicine. They're afraid they'll be alone. And I'll say, well, let's talk to your family about that, or I'll be here. I'll be checking on you.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I asked Pattie if anyone at the end of that list says, well, I'm just afraid of dying. I fear death. She said yes. And she listens if they want to talk about it, offers to bring in the chaplain or the social worker. What else is there? That might be the biggest thing that she and the other nurses know that we don't. They know the limits of what they can do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nancy Updike is one of the producers of our show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, since the federal government can no longer count on cartoon characters to bring in our tax dollars as they once did, what is left for them? My answer is in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose a theme. Today's program-- death and taxes, stories about the inevitable, stories where people who know about these things share their inside knowledge with us. In Act 1, we heard all about death. We have now arrived at Act 2, which is about taxes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think most of us think of taxes as inevitable like death. But in fact, while we all die, we do not all pay our taxes. According to the most recent statistics, the IRS only successfully collects 85% of the money that all of us owe, which is a lot of money. They miss $385 billion out of $2.6 trillion they should be collecting. Though when you think about it, what is amazing is how many of us actually do pay. There are entire countries where it seems like most people are cheating. Greece, I'm looking at you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here, we pay up, most of us, because of some combination of, A, we think we don't have a choice-- though if you'd bother to look into it, you would learn that the IRS does not have that many people checking on us-- and B, we think it's the right thing to do. NPR's David Kestenbaum has this story about how we got here and about one former IRS special agent trying, even in retirement, to help Uncle Sam in this quest.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The first year the government tried to collect an income tax from broad swaths of Americans was during World War II. And really, it was unclear how well it was going to work. One poll showed that one third to one half of people weren't sure what they were supposed to do.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And the government faced this choice. There were basically two options. The government could play tough, say this is the law. You have to pay. It could scare people. Or it could try to inspire people to pay their taxes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We went with inspire. We chose a spokesperson who could sell the income tax, someone with credibility, someone who was instantly recognizable and easy to understand.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: That is not right!

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We went with Donald Duck. This is a short film by Disney from 1942, commissioned by the government. In it, Donald Duck is marching around his house patriotically, listening to the radio, and talking back to it.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Your country needs you.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: OK!

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Donald Duck runs and gets a gun and a sword and an axe and boxing gloves.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Are you a patriotic American--

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Yes, sir!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: --eager to do your part?

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Yes, sir!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Then there's something important you can do.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Oh, boy. Oh, boy. Oh, boy. I'll do it.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: You won't get a medal for doing it.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Oh, that's all right.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: It may mean a sacrifice on your part.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: I'll do it anyway.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: But it will be a vital help to your country in this hour of need.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: I'll do anything! Anything!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Shall I tell you what it is?

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Yes! What is it? Tell me!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Shall I?

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Tell me what it is!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Your income tax.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Income tax?

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: [POP]

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Yes, your income tax.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Doggone income tax.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: They walk him through filing his whole tax return.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: You made less than $3,000 last year?

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Yes, sir!

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Well, then you can use the new simplified form.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Donald Duck writes in occupation-- actor. Income-- $2,501. He lists his dependents, three-- Huey, Dewey, and Louie.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Huey, Dewey, and Louie.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: They have him look up how much he owes in the tax tables.

segments.speaker: Donald Duck
segments.text: Oh, I owe just about--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This film was nominated for an Academy Award. And remarkably, this approach worked. Millions of Americans became responsible income taxpayers for the first time. Of course, when you're fighting the Nazis and you've got Donald Duck making the pitch, it's an easy sell. During the war, almost 90% of Americans polled said their taxes were fair. After the war, that plunged to around 60%.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: These days, some of us aren't so convinced of our duty. A recent survey by the IRS showed something like 1 in 10 people felt it was OK to cheat a little here and there or as much as possible on their taxes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is the taxpaying world that Al Drucker discovered when he started working for the IRS in 1981. He'd just graduated from John Jay College of Criminal Justice, and he was hoping to land a job at the FBI, or maybe the DEA, chasing drug traffickers. But the way things worked is, you just took this general aptitude test, and you waited to see who called. And the call he got was from the IRS.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Was it my peak choice? No. If I was in that recruiting forum and there were 20 booths, and one was DEA, and one was IRS, I'd probably go to the IRS last.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al didn't really even know the IRS hired law-enforcement people. But he took the job. They trained him to shoot a gun. They taught him special driving pursuit skills. And they gave him an impressive-looking badge that said Special Agent Number 4158, with the seal of the US Treasury on it. And he got to work.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One of Al's first cases came from a tip. It was a tip about a guy who ran a pharmacy in New Jersey. Someone had told the IRS, hey, you should check this guy out. I'm pretty sure he's cheating on his taxes. So Al, with a colleague, went to the pharmacy.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: And it was an old-fashioned-type pharmacy, a regular prescription-bearing pharmacy that would sell newspapers and gum and any of the stationery and cards, greeting cards and things of this nature.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Even in retirement, Al still speaks like a cop-- things of this nature, the suspect, the informant. Anyway, Al and his partner walk into the pharmacy, and the pharmacist is there. And they get the strangest reception.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Believe it or not, he looked at my partner and myself. And he looked at us, and he said, you guys are with the IRS, aren't you? As if he was expecting a visit.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Which, of course, he might have been. Someone, after all, had ratted him out. That was why Al was looking into this guy. And it was probably someone the pharmacist knew pretty well.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: It may be an employee. Sometimes an employee will brag about, when they're fired, turning the boss in, et cetera, et cetera.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The insider tip. It was a powerful thing. Al looked into the pharmacist's bank records and pretty quickly found something fishy. The guy didn't seem to be depositing any cash. All the money came from checks and credit cards. And clearly, people had been buying gum and newspapers and greeting cards with cash. Where was all the cash going?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: We were able to establish that there was another secret bank account where the cash was going.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Where was the secret bank account?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Just a different bank than he typically used.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Oh, it wasn't--

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: No, it wasn't offshore. It wasn't-- no, it--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It was around the corner.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: It was a neighboring town, and it was a different bank than he typically would use.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Was it in his real name?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: It was in his real name.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [LAUGHS] It's just amazing how simple it is. Basically, his secret bank account was a bank account in his name, one town over. And when he got paid in cash at the pharmacy, he just deposited it there and never declared it.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: There's no question. I think a lot of times, it's not nearly as complex as you might think.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A lot of cases are like that, he says. The fraud is right there once you start looking. But you need a reason to start looking. In this case, it was the tip that gave him that reason.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Tip, of course, is a nice word for it. Ratting out is another. But this notion that good ideas could come from people telling on each other-- it stuck with Al. So a couple years ago, when he retired from the IRS, he set up a business built around this idea, that people could help the government do its job collecting taxes by volunteering information. And here, for once, he did not give it a cop-speak name.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: TaxSqueal.com.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's not subtle. You went straight to squeal.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Those are the two words that best connote what I was trying to say, which is taxes and squealing. It could have been tax rat. And, well, we experimented plenty with the tax rat, believe me.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I suppose tax rat, you could have had a rat on the site. Tax squeal, you could have a pig.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Well, if I could be honest, the name was taken.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The IRS does have a way you can rat or squeal on other people. But like all things IRS, it's a pain.

segments.speaker: Female Voice
segments.text: Welcome to the Internal Revenue Service Tax Fraud Referral Hotline.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There's a hotline. But if you call, you get this.

segments.speaker: Female Voice
segments.text: You can report tax fraud and abuse by completing Form 3949-A or by sending us a letter.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Of course there's a form. You have to print it out, fill it out, and actually put it in an envelope and mail it to the IRS in Fresno. TaxSqueal.com, Al says, removes the hassle and provides an extra layer of anonymity. You just go to the website, type in some answers-- basically, who are you squealing on, where does the person live, what did they do? And that's it. Al will file the form for you for free.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al works out of the back of a store his wife runs in a New Jersey strip mall. The store is a little hard to describe. One side, literally one side of it, is devoted to sports memorabilia-- jerseys, photos, baseball cards. The other side is window treatments--

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: You have a blind that goes up, a blind that goes down, and certainly a blind that tilts.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: --making this, I think, the only store in America where you can buy baseball cards and window shades and squeal on your neighbor. Al works at a desk in back with his old badge, now preserved in a Lucite block, and some squeals he's printed out. When enough of them pile up, he mails them to the IRS.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al says the IRS-- despite what you might think, it's not all powerful. When he worked there, the IRS had only around 3,000 field agents doing criminal investigations. They are massively outmatched. So the IRS faces this fundamental problem. How do you find the cheaters?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al's answer, rat them out-- it may sound unpleasant. But it turns out this is one of the oldest tricks we've got. During the Civil War, we had an income tax on the rich for a while. And the government made it so that you could see exactly how much everyone was paying. The idea was that neighbors could rat out the guy next door if he lived on a big estate and didn't seem to be paying much. Squealing was the original form of tax enforcement.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The IRS today has a whistleblower program where they reward people for turning in big fish. Last year, the program paid out $53 million in awards. For smaller squeals, you can print out that form, fill it out, and mail it in. Or there's TaxSqueal.com.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: This goes. Let's see what's come in recently.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al reads through some of the stuff he's gotten through his website. There's someone squealing on jai alai gamblers in Florida. There's a retired sheriff ratting out a hair salon. There's one angry one in all caps, and a woman saying her ex-husband is claiming the kids as dependents when she's supposed to be. Actually, Al says there are a lot of exes-- ex-wives, ex-friends, ex-employees.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Dr. So-and-so had a dental office installed in the farm in Ohio and would routinely work on Amish and Mennonite patients on the weekends and off days. And those patients paid fully in cash. He would then not include those transactions as part of the regular business income. He would also trade and barter for services and not share those with his staff, who was paid on commission.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al doesn't check the validity of these allegations. He doesn't look into them at all. He just prints them out and mails them in. But if you want to pay just $2, Al does offer one extra service. For $2, Al will mail a little postcard to the person you've squealed on. Postcard is yellow with big black letters that read, you've been squealed on, exclamation point. On the back is a legal disclaimer saying, Tax Squeal is not a government entity, and explaining the Tax Squeal mission. He shows one to me and producer Chana Joffe-Walt.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: We have these nifty little postcards that say, you've been squealed on. And this will get mailed out.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's like a little extra "screw you."

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: [SIGH] Yes, it is. But it gives people another opportunity to get this information forward.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it's a way to really scare somebody who's not paying their taxes.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: If they haven't, that's exactly right. If you have, then it's not an issue.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No, I think that would scare me even if I had paid my taxes.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Maybe. Maybe--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You don't think so? You don't think people-- anybody who gets that is freaked out by it, even if they're completely compliant?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: Yeah, I guess you would be frightened. I guess you would be frightened. I don't look at it that way. But yeah, the average person would probably be frightened.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So what do you think about that?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: I think if you've done what you should do, you don't worry about it. If you haven't, well, you have the possibility of cleaning up your act before somebody comes knocking on your door.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Honestly, I was conflicted about all this. It felt kind of wrong, but I can't say why. Maybe it's that if you turn someone in, you worry that bad things are going to happen to them.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One time I was in this little corner grocery store, and I saw this woman shoplifting. And I went back and forth about whether I should say something. In the end, I did. But my heart was pounding. And as I left I heard the store owner confronting her, and I just felt awful. Squealing-- it doesn't feel like something to be proud of. An Al-- even Al-- he's got complicated feelings about it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How do you feel about squealing?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: If you feel strongly enough about a certain situation, I think you should report it. It's as simple as that. My own personal belief-- would I do it? No.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You wouldn't use your own website?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: I would be-- no, I wouldn't do it. I just wouldn't do it, because I don't think-- I just wouldn't do it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: It's just not my nature to do those kind of thing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Because it feels wrong to you to turn them in?

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: No, it's just not something I would do. It's not wrong or right.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: No, it's got to be right. It's got to be right to turn them in if they're doing something wrong.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: It really depends. It depends on the situation. I would have to be directly affected before I would do something like that. I wouldn't do it. I'd sooner approach the person before I did this. The anonymous feature makes it very suspect.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You're allowing people to do this thing that you yourself wouldn't do.

segments.speaker: Al Drucker
segments.text: I'm giving the ability to do it. Doesn't mean I choose to do it, right?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Al's Tax Squeal business is not going as well as he'd hoped. The tax attorneys he thought would pay to advertise on the website? They didn't really materialize. And that $2 "you've been squealed on" postcard service? Most people don't do it. Most people, it turns out, are like Al. They don't want to squeal. Sure, there are lots of vindictive ex-employees and ex-spouses out there eager to squeal, just maybe not enough to support a business. Al says the postage alone is killing him.

segments.text: You're going to smell more bad. You're going to sweat. Sweating more, a lot more.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Chest hair. Chest hair.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Getting really smelly.

segments.speaker: Janah Boccio
segments.text: Chest hair.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sweating like a moose.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
